sentences.text: Federal reports from the 1980s described health promotion as involving three key mechanisms: self-care (decisions and actions individuals take for their own health), mutual aid (actions people take to help each other cope), and healthy environments (creation of conditions and surroundings conducive to health).

Four strategies were used by the Health Promotion Directorate: equipping the public to deal with lifestyle issues through informational activities; promoting a social climate that supports healthy lifestyles through advertising and promotional work; supporting self-help and citizen participation in health promotion through joint projects with voluntary organizations; and promoting the involvement of health care, social welfare, and other established programs in health promotion.

Direct communication with the public was achieved through media advertising, promotional activities, and distribution of information, with the most significant advertising programs being Generation of Non-Smokers, Dialogue on Drinking, and Stay Real, a cannabis information project.

Health promotion activities included education, training, research, legislation, policy coordination and community development, and by the mid 1970s, health promotion activities were becoming more visible in schools, community health services, drug and alcohol commissions and in the workplace.

Several programs of national scope were in operation by the 1980s, including Dialogue on Drinking, the Breast-Feeding Program, It's Just Your Nerves (a program on women's use of alcohol and tranquillizers), Time to Quit (a smoking-cessation program), Stay Real (a drug information program), and Break Free (aimed at reducing smoking among young people).

The Health Promotion program was divided into 12 components: five components addressed lifestyle issues (nutrition, smoking, alcohol use, drug use and hypertension); four components addressed the concerns of particular population groups (children and youth, women, the elderly, and the disabled); and three components addressed functions or methods of delivery (communications, school health and health promotion in the workplace).

Federal reports noted that health promotion had relied heavily upon the dissemination of health information, but this approach produced only slight and slow shifts in attitudes and health behaviour, leading to the recognition that information campaigns should be combined with a variety of other activities.

A 1984 federal report noted that while health promotion was practised by both governments and non-government organizations, their fragmentation had resulted in a poorly coordinated or integrated health promotion infrastructure, and no health goals had been set nationally for health promotion as there had been in the United States.
